title: Potential difference and emf; Electrical power and energy
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EL05-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; EL02-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; EL05-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; EL05-1#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EL02-1#N.3a, EL05-1#N.3, EL02-1#N.6, EL05-1#N.5, EL02-1#N.13a, EL05-1#N.10b, EL05-1#N.11a.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Power
items.clue: Rate of energy transfer, which can be found from I²R.

items.label: Volt
items.clue: Unit meaning 1 J transferred for each coulomb passing between two places.

items.label: Series
items.clue: Arrangement in which a kettle element and its cable carry the same current.

items.label: Heating effect
items.clue: Rise in temperature as electrons pass energy to lattice ions, making them vibrate more.

questions.stem: A steady current of 0.50 A flows through a small electric motor for 2.0 minutes. In this time, 360 J of energy is transferred from electrical energy to other forms in the motor. What is the potential difference across the motor?

The potential difference across an ohmic resistor is increased so that the current in the resistor becomes three times as large. What is the ratio of the new power dissipated in the resistor, P₂, to the original power, P₁?
questions.explanation: The resistor is ohmic, so R is unchanged. P = I²R: tripling I multiplies P by 3² = 9.

questions.stem: Predict first. A cell has an emf of 1.5 V. What does this mean?

options.text: The cell holds a store of 1.5 C of charge, which it releases into the circuit.
The cell pushes each coulomb of charge around the circuit with a force of 1.5 N.
For each coulomb passing through the cell, 1.5 J is transferred to electrical energy.
The cell drives a current of 1.5 A through any circuit connected to it.

questions.stem: A steady current of 0.25 A flows in a 24 Ω resistor for 2.0 minutes. How much energy is dissipated in the resistor?
questions.explanation: Power = I²R = 0.25² × 24 = 1.5 W. Energy = power × time = 1.5 W × 120 s = 180 J.

questions.stem: A battery of emf 12 V drives a steady current of 40 A through a starter motor for 1.5 s. How much energy does the battery transfer to the charge that passes through it in this time?
questions.explanation: Charge: q = It = 40 × 1.5 = 60 C. Each coulomb gains 12 J, so energy = emf × q = 12 × 60 = 720 J.

questions.stem: A 60 W lamp and a 100 W lamp are both designed to work on the same 230 V supply. Which lamp has the larger resistance when working normally, and why?

options.text: The 100 W lamp, as a higher power needs a larger resistance.
Both are the same, as they are designed for the same supply pd.
The 60 W lamp, as at the same pd a smaller R gives more power.
The 100 W lamp, as P = I²R and it takes the larger current.

questions.explanation: At the same pd, P = V²/R. R = 230²/60 ≈ 880 Ω for the 60 W lamp and 230²/100 ≈ 530 Ω for the 100 W lamp.

questions.stem: A 60 W lamp and a 100 W lamp are both rated for a 230 V supply. They are connected in series across a 230 V supply. Assume each keeps its normal working resistance. Which lamp is brighter?

options.text: The 60 W lamp: it has the larger resistance, and in series both carry the same current.
The 100 W lamp: it has the higher power rating, so it gives more light.
The 100 W lamp: a smaller resistance gives more power, as P = V²/R.
Both are equally bright, as they carry the same current.

questions.explanation: R = V²/P: about 880 Ω for the 60 W lamp, 530 Ω for the 100 W lamp. Same current in series, so P = I²R is larger in the 60 W lamp (about 23 W against 14 W).
